title: The Courtesy Clause
logline: Marshall takes Ted's four-hundred-dollar small claims case over a doghouse the dog won't enter, and finds his law-school best friend Brad across the aisle. They swear the friendship is safe under their old Courtesy Clause (fist bump before, high five after, split a sandwich at recess), but a judge who rewards playing nice turns every courtesy into a weapon, until Marshall refuses the one gesture that was never a tactic.

guests.name: Rosalind Fiore
guests.role: The defendant, Brad's elderly landlady, who refused to pay Ted for the doghouse. Speaks about her small white bichon Pancake like he's a sensitive stage actor between roles

guests.name: Judge Dolores Kaminski
guests.role: Small claims judge and former middle school vice principal of nineteen years. Runs her courtroom like a cafeteria: rewards whoever plays nice, sees through everyone, and can reduce a grown man to seventh grade with one word

facts.brad.landlady: Rosalind Fiore, who pays him in Sunday lasagna
facts.brad.sourdough: Brad keeps a sourdough starter named Big Marsh
facts.ted.pavilion: built Mrs. Fiore a canine pavilion; lost the $400 small claims suit

opens.note: Marshall and Brad's pact when they face off in court: fist bump before, high five after, split a sandwich at recess
Judge Dolores Kaminski, ex-vice principal, small claims; Barney is terrified of her and obeys her instantly

scenes.summary: Over the stoop, Future Ted sets up 'the most important case of his career'; inside, it's four hundred dollars. Ted's canine pavilion, Pancake the philistine. Brad knocks, hugs, hands over the papers: he represents his landlady. The Courtesy Clause flashback to Columbia, 2002 (ketchup packets, half a meatball sub). They renew it with a fist bump. Button: Marshall rattles off Brad's weaknesses far too fast.

beats.line: In the spring of 2011, your Uncle Marshall took on the most important case of his career.
Four hundred dollars? Ted, I sue chemical companies. My last case had a river in it.
And this one has a principle in it. Mrs. Fiore won't pay because her dog won't go inside.
Why won't the dog go inside?
Because Pancake is a philistine.
Buddy. Is it possible you built a weird doghouse?
It is not a doghouse. It's a canine pavilion.
What's the difference?
About three hundred dollars in cedar.
I'm in. I haven't argued in a real courtroom since my zoning appeal for Bigfoot habitat.
Big Marsh!
Bro, I wanted you to hear this from me.
You're representing Mrs. Fiore?
She has a lawyer? For four hundred dollars?
She's my landlady. Rent-stabilized. I would help that woman bury a body.
What's she paying you?
Lasagna. Every Sunday. Lily, it has a béchamel layer.
Brad. You know what this means.
The Courtesy Clause.
The what?
First week of law school, I lost my wallet. I lived on ketchup packets for four days.
Dude. Are you eating a ketchup packet?
It's tomato soup if you believe in yourself.
Half a meatball sub. No strings.
Brad, if we ever end up on opposite sides of a courtroom—
Fist bump before. High five after. And at recess, we split a sandwich.
No matter what.
Whatever happens in that courtroom stays in that courtroom.
Bro. It's a doghouse.
Pavilion.
See you in court, buddy. Bring snacks.
Okay. Just so we're prepared. What are his weaknesses?
He can't take a compliment, he can't resist a dog in a sweater, and he cries at proposal videos.
Why did I have that ready?

scenes.summary: Judge Kaminski, ex-vice principal: she notices who plays nice, and gum. Barney regresses to seventh grade; Lily spots a 'sticker lady'. Brad initiates the fist bump and gets the credit; Marshall extended second. Ted's Exhibit A, the reading nook, and Pancake's use of the corner. Marshall's objection is sustained and Brad high-fives him for it, which the judge loves. Button: Lily, narrow-eyed: he's good.

beats.line: Mosby versus Fiore. Before we begin, I was a middle school vice principal for nineteen years.
I notice who plays nice. I notice who doesn't. And I notice gum.
Vice principal eyes. I'm in seventh grade again. I can feel my retainer.
Oh. She's a sticker lady.
Counselor.
Look at that. Mr. Morris, extending the hand of friendship. Noted.
I also extended, Your Honor. It was a mutual extension.
You extended second.
The plaintiff calls Ted Mosby. Architect.
A modest structure, Your Honor. I lost money on the clerestory.
beats.title: Exhibit A: The Fiore Canine Pavilion

beats.line: Why does a dog need a reading nook?
Pancake will never read if nobody believes in him, Your Honor.
Mr. Mosby. Has Pancake ever gone inside your doghouse?
Pavilion.
Has Pancake ever gone inside your pavilion?
He's engaged with it.
Engaged how?
He uses the corner.
Uses it for what, Mr. Mosby?
For what dogs use corners for, Brad!
Objection! Counsel is badgering the architect.
Sustained. No badgering, no running, no gum.
Great objection, buddy.
Mr. Morris. Gracious in defeat. Noted.
I won. I won, and he high fived me, and somehow he's winning.
Focus, Marshall. He's being mean to my pavilion.
Oh, he's good.

scenes.summary: Marshall fumes about the high five. Barney: graceful losing is the most aggressive act. Lily: a sticker judge rewards the kid who shares loudest. Barney's Playbook page, The Gracious Assassin. Marshall refuses, then asks how long to hug. Robin defects: Brad prepped her over brunch. Barney has waited years for Marshall to go full shark. Button: Lily already made a chart.

beats.line: I won the objection, and he high fived me. Who does that?
A genius. Losing gracefully in public is the most aggressive thing a man can do.
I've lost at darts to forty different boyfriends. I'm undefeated with their girlfriends.
Baby, she's a sticker lady. Every school has one. Gold stars for sharing.
I've watched five-year-olds hand over a crayon while making eye contact with me. Brad is that kid.
So what do I do?
You share louder.
The Gracious Assassin. I once used it to win a divorce I wasn't even in.
beats.title: The Gracious Assassin
lines: Hug your opponent. Longer than he wants.
Compliment him where the judge can hear.
Lose one small thing on purpose.
Be the bigger man. Literally. You're six foot four.

beats.line: No. Brad is my friend. I am not going to hug my friend strategically.
How long is longer than he wants?
Eight count. Make eye contact with the judge on five.
Full disclosure, I'm on Brad's side now.
What?
He subpoenaed me. I saw Pancake reject your pavilion. We did witness prep over brunch.
He made hollandaise from scratch, Ted. You made a dog a library.
Marshall, I have waited six years for this. The big friendly Minnesotan, finally going full shark.
I'm not going full shark. I'm being nice. Aggressively. To my friend.
Lily, what does Brad hate more, getting out-hugged or out-complimented?
Baby, I already made a chart.

scenes.label: Day two
scenes.summary: Marshall arrives and hugs Brad for an eight count. Compliment war: kind eyes, Greek statue calves. Marshall's stakeout in a hedge with Barney. Triumphant score as he unveils Exhibit B: Pancake in the pavilion. It's a raccoon. Brad: so was your Bigfoot photo; he'd said inconclusive to be nice. Robin testifies that Pancake was embarrassed for Ted. Recess.

beats.line: Brad! My friend! Bring it in!
That's an eight count. That's my boy.
That was a lot of hug.
Your Honor, may I say, opposing counsel has the kindest eyes in the five boroughs.
And may I say, opposing counsel has the calves of a Greek statue.
Thanks, bro. I've been doing walking lunges.
Gentlemen. Calves are not evidence.
Then let's talk evidence. Last night, I obtained a photograph.
Come on, Pancake. Go see your pavilion.
Why am I in a hedge?
You said you wanted to see me go full shark.
In a courtroom! Sharks don't live in hedges!
Exhibit B, Your Honor. Pancake, inside the pavilion, at four in the morning.
Mr. Eriksen. This is a raccoon.
With respect, Your Honor, that is a small white dog who has had a very long night.
Pancake doesn't wear a little mask.
Marshall. Buddy. Your Bigfoot photo was also a raccoon.
You told me it was inconclusive!
I was being nice!
The defense calls Robin Scherbatsky.
Miss Scherbatsky, what did Pancake do when he first saw the pavilion?
He sniffed the reading nook. He looked at Ted. Then he walked out into the rain and lay down in a puddle.
How would you describe his expression?
Embarrassed. For Ted.
Robin!
I'm under oath, Ted. Also, sorry.
We'll break for lunch.

scenes.label: Lunch recess
scenes.summary: Brad brings half a meatball sub, per the Clause. Future Ted says Marshall politely declined; the sanitized version plays. Luke and Penny call it. The truth: Marshall accuses Brad of a food-coma tactic before closing. Brad admits the high five was a move. The sandwich wasn't. Marshall doesn't believe him. Brad leaves him holding it.

beats.line: Half a meatball sub. Like old times.
And your Uncle Marshall politely declined.
Brad, that's so thoughtful. But I couldn't possibly.
Totally get it, buddy.
Uncle Marshall has never said I couldn't possibly about a sandwich.
Last Thanksgiving he finished a sandwich I was still holding.
Fine. That's not exactly what he said.
Meatball. At twelve thirty. You know I crash at two.
What?
Closing is at two fifteen, Brad. You're trying to put me in a meat coma.
Marshall. It's the Clause. It's a sandwich.
Nothing's just a sandwich with you! The fist bump was a move. The high five was a move!
Yeah. The high five was a move.
The sandwich wasn't.
I don't believe you.
Then don't eat it.

scenes.summary: Nine hours later Marshall is still holding the uneaten sandwich. Ted is still wounded about the puddle. Robin knocks: Brad's witness prep was mostly about Marshall, the only guy at Columbia who asked about his sourdough instead of his biceps. The starter is named Big Marsh. Lily owns her chart; Marshall owns his need to win, even at being nice. He finally takes a bite.

beats.line: Baby, you've been holding that sandwich for nine hours.
If I eat it, he wins. If I don't, I'm a man who didn't eat a sandwich. I don't know that man.
Can we take one moment for my pavilion, which a Canadian called embarrassing under oath?
She said the dog was embarrassed.
For me, Lily! The dog was embarrassed for me!
Hey. There's something you should know about Brad's witness prep.
He poisoned you with hollandaise.
Prep was two hours. Pancake took ten minutes. The rest was you.
Your Fiero. Your dad. The futon you carried up five flights. He does a really good impression of you.
He does me?
He hugs whoever's closest and says, oh, buddy.
He said you were the only guy at Columbia who asked about his sourdough instead of his biceps.
He's very proud of that starter.
He named it after you. It's called Big Marsh.
Marshmallow, this is my fault. I made a chart of your best friend's weaknesses.
It was a really good chart.
But it's not the chart, Lilypad. I didn't want to win the case. I wanted to beat Brad. At being nice.
Who tries to win at being nice?
Your mother. Every Thanksgiving.
Oh no. He put the good peppers on it.

scenes.label: Day three
scenes.summary: Closing: Marshall puts on the record that he was nice to win, and that he missed the one time Brad was just nice. Judge Kaminski knew from the first fist bump; she gave Brad the points for the high five anyway. On the merits, Ted swore eleven times he built a pavilion, not the doghouse he was hired for: judgment for the defendant, and Ted is thrilled. Barney's gum. The gang files out; Marshall brings Brad a turkey sandwich. A move, to get his friend back. Big Marsh is rising. Hug, high five after, and the two of them sit side by side at Marshall's table, sharing it.

beats.line: Closing arguments. Mr. Eriksen.
Your Honor, for two days, opposing counsel and I have been extremely nice to each other.
I'd like the record to show I was doing it to win.
I hugged him for an eight count. I complimented his calves. I sat in a hedge with Barney.
And the one time he was just being nice, I told him I didn't believe him.
I'm sorry, Brad. I ate it. You put the good peppers on it.
I always put the good peppers on it.
Mr. Eriksen, I ran a middle school for nineteen years. I knew at the first fist bump.
Mr. Morris. That high five.
Total move, Your Honor.
I know. I gave you the points anyway. It was a very clean five.
Now, the merits. Mr. Mosby, you were hired to build a doghouse. Under oath, you corrected that word eleven times.
By your own sworn testimony, you never built a doghouse. You built a pavilion. Judgment for the defendant.
Pancake thanks you, Your Honor. He'll be in touch.
Marshall. She called it a pavilion.
Ted, you lost four hundred dollars.
On the record, Marshall. Pavilion.
Mr. Stinson. Gum.
It's been in since Tuesday, ma'am. I was too scared to move it.
You were one hedge away from greatness.
Go.
Clause says high five after.
Clause says sandwich at recess. I'm calling a recess.
It's turkey. Nobody's crashing at two.
Is this a move?
Yeah. I'm trying to get my friend back.
Robin told you about the starter, didn't she?
How's Big Marsh doing?
Rising beautifully.
